messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] method = "mr" not working
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] method = "mr" not working
messages.body_plain:
method="mr" uses only fully-informative marker genotypes; for a 4-way cross, markers are almost always partially informative, and so most all information gets omitted.

If you're getting good results from method="em" or method="hk", I'd stick with them.

karl

messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Distance matrix from genetic map
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Karl. That is exactly what I was looking for. Here's a simple code example:

###### Distance matrix from an R/qtl cross.object

# Calculate similarity between genotypes
similarity_matrix<-comparegeno(cross.object)

# Add in the RIL line names as row and col names
rownames(similarity_matrix)<-cross.object$pheno[,1]
colnames(similarity_matrix)<-cross.object$pheno[,1]

# Transform similarity matrix into difference matrix
inverted<-similarity_matrix - 1
distance_matrix<-inverted * -1

# Replace 'NA' with 0 (Identical RILs have 0 distance between them)
distance_matrix[is.na <http://is.na>(distance_matrix)]<-0

# Can now use to examine dendrogram of RILs
hc<-hclust(as.dist(distance_matrix))
plot(hc, cex=0.45)

###### END

I'm trying to compare 2 genetic maps of the same RIL self population constructed using different genotyping technologies. They appear almost identical, but any discrepancy between them will be interesting to examine further.

Two ways I can think of doing this is comparing the number and location of breakpoints (XO) within each RIL per build and looking at how similar/different the RILs are from each other as a whole between map assemblies.

Any other suggestions/methods would be greatly appreciated. Thanks again,

Max

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Get the p-value for all SNPs in QTL calculation
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Get the p-value for all SNPs in QTL calculation
messages.body_plain:
The p-value is the proportion of permutations with LOD score greater than or equal to the observed LOD, so you could go through the LODs for each SNP and calculate those proportions.

# example analysis and permutations
data(fake.bc)
fake.bc <- calc.genoprob(fake.bc, step=2.5)
out <- scanone(fake.bc, method="hk")
operm <- scanone(fake.bc, method="hk", n.perm=1000)

# calculate p-values
pval <- sapply(out[,3], function(a,b) mean(b >= a), operm)

# the same thing, via a for loop
pval <- rep(NA, nrow(out))
for(i in 1:nrow(out))
    pval[i] <- mean(operm >= out[i,3])

karl

messages.subject: Re: Experiment-wise error rate control across many phenotypes
messages.subject_clean: Experiment-wise error rate control across many phenotypes
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl et al.
I wanted to bring this discussion up again :
How do we deal with the multiple testing problem across many phenotypes (>1000)?
The permutation approach does a nice job of controlling the family-wise error rate for a single trait, however, with many traits, the experiment-wise error rate is no longer controlled. How do we solve this?

The way I see it, there are two solutions, although there may be many others. Please let me know what you think is the best approach:
1) Run sets of permutations many times, each time extracting the LOD threshold of interest. With a distribution of LOD thresholds, take the 95th% threshold (or some other threshold depending on the number of traits) as your new cutoff.
2) For each trait, calculate a p-value based on the LOD score (as described below) and do FDR on these. Thus, retaining only QTL that exceed a p-value cutoff.

Any advice is appreciated.
John

On Wednesday, September 26, 2012 at 10:47:28 AM UTC-5, Karl Broman wrote:
> With just one phenotype and no X-chromosome-specific permutations, you could just do something like this:
>
>   data(fake.bc)
>   fake.bc <- calc.genoprob(fake.bc)
>   out <- scanone(fake.bc, method="hk")
>   operm <- scanone(fake.bc, method="hk", n.perm=1000)
>   pval <- sapply(out[,3], function(a,b) mean(b >= a), opera)
>
> In place of sapply in that last line, you could use a for loop:
>
>   pval <- rep(NA, nrow(out))
>   for(i in 1:nrow(out))
>      pval[i] <- mean(operm >= out[i,3])
>
> But these are p-values adjusting for the genome scan (and so controlling the family-wise error rate, FWER).
>
> It's not clear to me exactly what sort of p-values you want, for your FDR calculations.
>
> I'd recommend against using FDR control for the scan across genome, but I can see using it to handle the multiple phenotypes, if you have *many* phenotypes (like 20,000).  But in that case I'd focus on a single p-value per phenotype.
>
> karl
>
> On Sep 26, 2012, at 10:23 AM, Annette <annette...@gmx.net> wrote:
>
> > Dear Karl,
> >
> > I’m conducting an QTL study in a mouse intercross.  A challenge is figuring out how to control for multiple testing with many phenotypes (we have n=1841).  One method is using q-values/FDRs based on permutations: to use the package q-value (Storey et al, 2003) I require a list of p-values (instead of LOD-scores) for my R/qtl scanone results for each phenotype.
> >
> >
> > Is there any way to get a p-value for each marker (as I get for the LOD-scores), instead of the summary function (which I used below), where I just get the highest LOD-score for each chromosome?
> >
> >
> > for(k in 1:(length(cross0$pheno))) {
> > out.1=  scanone(cross0, pheno.col=2, method="em", model="normal")
> > operm.f2<- scanone(cross0, pheno.col=2, method="em", model="normal" , n.perm=1000)

> > write.csv(a,file = paste("C:/Documents and Settings/rQTL_outputFiles_pvalues/pvalues_",names(cross0$pheno[k]),".txt",sep=""))

I wanted to bring this discussion up again :
How do we deal with the multiple testing problem across many phenotypes (>1000)?
The permutation approach does a nice job of controlling the

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Experiment-wise error rate control across many phenotypes
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Experiment-wise error rate control across many phenotypes
messages.body_plain:
(2) would work (control for genome scan at each trait, and then control FDR across traits).

But (1) won't work: in many cases, the LOD thresholds for different traits will be about the same, so taking 95th percentile of these won't control for the search across traits.

Rather, to control family-wise error rate (for genome scans, and then across the traits), you'd need to do a permutation test with all traits; at each permutation replicate, write down the genome-wide maximum LOD for each trait. This gives a matrix of size n_perm x n_pheno.

If traits all have about the same LOD threshold, you could then take the maximum across traits for each permutation replicate, and then use the 95%ile of these maximum: that would be FWER control for both genome and traits.

A related idea that accounts for differences in LOD threshold across traits is described in the following paper (see right column of page 118):

  https://www.biostat.wisc.edu/~kbroman/publications/burrage.pdf

karl

messages.subject_clean: how to set parameters in orderMarkers?
messages.body_plain:
hello everyone. I'm constructing a gentic map for a fish with about 5300 SNP markers and 110 samples. After estimating RF(with est.rf()), I got the chromosome number exactly the same to the number of halpotype. the command I used is
lg <- formLinkageGroups(jiyu3, max.rf=0.35, min.lod=11)

But I found the length of LG is too large. For example, in a LG with 69 markers, the length of it is about 900cm. There is a gap larger than 500 cm within it .
The command I used is :

jiyu3<- orderMarkers(jiyu3, chr=48,map.function="kosambi",maxit=10000,sex.sp=FALSE,tol=1e-6)

Now I want to know how to set  map.function, maxit and tol in this function.
Is there any way to speed up the orderMarkers?

Thanks

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] how to set parameters in orderMarkers?
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] how to set parameters in orderMarkers?
messages.body_plain:
In my experience, it's unlikely that you'll get the same number of linkage groups as there are chromosomes without making any mistakes. I generally start with more linkage groups than there are chromosomes and merge some later.

The large 500 cM gap in a linkage group likely indicates that that group should be split into two.

With orderMarkers(), the defaults for map.function, maxit, and tol, are probably fine.
If you want to speed it up, start with making the 'window' argument smaller. Making 'maxit' smaller or 'tol' bigger will also speed it up.

karl

messages.body_plain:
> So, in the case of quantile normalized traits - with identical distributions - replicating permutations would be OK.

I'm not sure I understand.

In the case that the traits have identical marginal distributions, as with quantile normalized traits, one could do permutations with a single trait to get a significance threshold that could apply to any trait (when viewed individually).

But if you also want to control for the search across traits, then you need to take account of the correlations among traits, and so you need to do joint permutations, permuting the rows in the phenotype matrix relative to the rows in the genotype matrix.

I'm a little confused. Each row in the matrix I described is the set of genome-wide maximum LOD scores for all traits, for a single permutation of the traits relative to the genotypes. There are no cutoffs yet. The maximum for that row is the single-largest LOD score, across both the genome and the traits, for that single permutation replicate.

The 95th percentile of those row maxima is then a significance threshold for to control the error rate for the searches across both the genome and the traits.

The initial set of cutoffs don't account for the search across traits.

karl

> So again, I feel this is conservative since we don't just want the highest LOD trait in the study.

Formally, the procedure would only apply to the single-biggest LOD score, across the genome and across traits. But you could still use the threshold as a landmark in considering other LOD peaks, just as we do when looking at a genome scan: we consider other peaks aside from the biggest one. Or you could do something like the method in Chen and Storey (2005), http://www.genetics.org/content/173/4/2371.abstract

FWER control is inherently conservative, though one might say it's appropriately so.

>
> Alternatively, what is the downside of the following procedure?
> Estimate the distribution of LOD cutoffs when n_pheno are tested.
> Reject/accept LOD's based on some quantile of this distribution.
>
> At the moment, I feel this cutoff distribution exactly addresses the the search across traits.
>

Looking at the cutoff distribution just doesn't work, in seeking to control the search across traits. You were to use the number of traits to decide what significance level you might use in defining the cutoff, but then we're back to the FWER type thing, maybe via Bonferroni.

If you want something less conservative, I'd suggest switching to FDR control for the traits.

karl

Thank you for the response, Karl -- yes, I see.

E.g.,
Assume permutation distributions are identical for traits and can be perfectly estimated.
Every trait gets the same cutoff, and the distribution of cutoffs is degenerate at that value.
So this distribution has no relationship to controlling for multiple testing; rather, it just estimates the cutoff.

Okay.
So rather than take a cutoff, suppose we just take a single random sample from each permutation distribution.
Then a row in your matrix recapitulates the null component of a "two"-part mixture model of null=TRUE LOD scores and null=FALSE LOD scores.
It's not intuitive to me that this alone identifies the non-null component of the mixture (and the mixing proportion), but suppose it does.
We could then directly estimate FDR for study LOD scores.
Which is probably a long and unnecessary digression for me to say "oh, yes, I like FDR" on the way to the real question.

But before the real question, let me just surmise that (given reliable FDR and FWER), all you mean by "FWER control is inherently conservative, though one might say it's appropriately so" is that, e.g., FWER and FDR are inherently different measures, not that you necessarily subscribe to one or the other in the QTL context, right?

Okay.
As I understand it, the culmination of the current state of the thread is that given a set of LOD scores (pvalues), p.adjust(method="fdr") is a viable means to address multiple testing.

Suppose now we have multiple competing models from which we presumably select the most appropriate on a trait by trait basis. The traits are then partitioned by model they were fit with (but the LOD scores for all models fit on a given trait are retained).  For a set of traits partitioned together (i.e., fit with the same model), how do you feel about FDR (FWER) for these traits based upon the LODs of ALL traits when fit under this model? And subsequently, the analogous procedure for each set of traits partitioned together (i.e., fit with the same model)?

So, for example, suppose there are two models (A-B) and four traits (a-d) with model A chosen for traits a-b and model B chosen for traits c-d.

"LOD table"
    a(A)  b(A)  c(B)   d(B)
A
B

Then (for example) FDR for traits a-b is based on row A LODs, while FDR for traits c-d is based on row B LODs.
